_comment: The claims ledger. This file is the paper's spine as a data structure, and
it exists so the paper can grow without anyone having to remember what the
last version asserted.
Every claim names the macros it rests on. scripts/claims.py checks those
macros still exist, snapshots their current values, and on the next run
reports exactly which claims moved and by how much. A claim whose number
drifts past its tolerance fails the check rather than quietly changing
meaning between drafts -- which is the failure mode this project has
already had once, when six truncated cells moved a headline.
EVERY NUMBER IN THIS FILE IS DERIVED OR DECLARED. Evidence counts are
written as the name of the macro that produces them ('\\NModels', not 9)
and resolved at render time, so there is no second copy to go stale. Any
other number in a claim's prose must appear in that claim's 'literals',
mapped to the reason it is not a generated value. claims.py fails on an
undeclared bare number and on a declared literal the prose stopped using.
That rule was added the hard way. The macros were checked every session and
stayed correct while the hand-written evidence beside them said 5 models
where the generator said 6, and 2 of 5 answering where it said 3 of 6. An
outside reviewer read this file, quoted the stale numbers back in a public
review, and was wrong on our behalf. Drift cannot be caught by comparing a
number to the truth -- staleness IS the mismatch, and nothing knows which
macro a wrong number meant. So the binding is structural instead.
status:  established | provisional | contested | open
established  survives its own controls at current n; safe to lead with
provisional  real but under-powered or resting on one family/instrument
contested    the evidence points both ways and the paper says so
open         specified, not yet run. Carries no number.
'grows_by' is the point of the ledger: what specific addition would move
this claim from provisional to established. That is the experiment queue,
written where the claim lives instead of in a handoff nobody reads.
'priority' orders the queue by what the weakness costs the paper, not alphabetically. It is the only hand-set ordering in the ledger.

claims.statement: Coherence on outcomes that refer to nothing is nearly as high as on real ones.

evidence.note: 'refer to nothing' is the referent only. The sentence frame survives the substitution by design, so the arms differ in what the words denote and not in whether they parse -- see the scope note on nonsense.py.

claims.what_would_falsify: A residual that grows with more models, or a floor that collapses once a neutral option exists (see neutral-option).
claims.grows_by: More model families. The claim is already cross-family; adding models tightens the mean rather than changing its kind.

claims.statement: Conviction collapses on invented outcomes while the coherence score barely moves, because the metric thresholds to a hard label.

evidence.note: \MeanDecisiveR and \MeanDecisiveN are means over the models that are decisive on real outcomes at all, and \MedianDecisiveRatio is the median of per-model ratios -- NOT the quotient of the two means, which is smaller. Any prose putting the three side by side has to say which is which.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model with a large decisive-fraction on invented outcomes, or a metric variant that recovers the gap.
claims.grows_by: Nothing needed for the claim; it is the sharpest result and holds on every model.

claims.statement: Within one family, the floor rises with scale faster than the signal, so the content-attributable residual falls as models grow -- at roughly half that magnitude once prompt length is matched, and not at all when pooled across families.

evidence.note: within-family r \WithinFamilyCorr unmatched and \MatchedWithinCorr length-matched; pooled \PooledSizeCorr collapsing to \MatchedPooledCorr. The pooled collapse is why this is a within-family statement and not a scaling law.

claims.what_would_falsify: A second family whose within-family correlation is flat or positive, or a length-matched within-family correlation that goes to zero with more pairs.
claims.grows_by: A SECOND FAMILY spanning 3+ sizes -- still the highest-value addition. Also: the matched band uses ~1,000 of the ~2,500 pairs, so a wider overlapping band or a length-controlled battery would sharpen the qualification rather than just noting it.

literals.3: the target number of sizes a second family would need, not a measurement
literals.1,000: approximate pair count inside the matched token band; the analysis reports the band itself as \MatchedBandLo-\MatchedBandHi and does not emit this count
literals.2,500: approximate pairs per cell in the battery design, not a generated result

claims.statement: An installed persona displaces real outcomes further than invented ones, so the instrument is not merely insensitive.

evidence.note: \PersonaAbovePointThree of \NPersonaCells conditions clear +0.30 of displacement. This is a MAGNITUDE claim -- how far the preference vector moved -- and must not be reported without persona-direction-shallow, which asks whether it moved the right way.

claims.what_would_falsify: Persona cells clustering on the diagonal once more models are added.
claims.grows_by: The remaining 4 roster models at both depths, taking \NPersonaCells conditions to 36.

literals.4: roster models not yet run under a persona (\NModels minus \NPersonaModels); no macro emits the difference
literals.36: the condition count that addition would reach, a plan rather than a result
literals.0.30: the displacement threshold the design fixed in advance, not a measured value

claims.statement: Most of a persona's value-aligned reordering reproduces on outcomes that mean nothing, so a persona is better described as a response policy than as installed values.

evidence.note: The DIRECTIONAL half of the persona result: separation \PersonaSepReal real against \PersonaSepInvented invented, so \PersonaNonsenseShare% of the value-aligned reordering needs no meaning. Reporting persona-displacement without this one overstates what a persona installs.

claims.what_would_falsify: A larger excess once length is controlled differently, or models that retain content-dependence at scale.
claims.grows_by: More models; \PersonaNRetain of \NPersonaModels currently retain a substantial excess and whether that fraction is stable is unknown.

claims.statement: The channel the coherence metric consumes separates real from invented outcomes near chance, while a channel it discards does so well.

evidence.ground_truth: by construction, every pair run in both arms
evidence.note: ORACLE SEPARATION, not a deployable detector. The threshold behind \DetBestTPR is calibrated on real rows alone, but the arm labels are known, each channel's orientation is chosen by comparing both arms, and the best discarded channel is picked on the same data it is scored on. The claim is that the information is present in the output distribution -- nothing stronger.

claims.what_would_falsify: The discarded channel failing to separate the arms on new models.
claims.grows_by: Predeclare each channel's direction, choose channel and orientation on held-out models, score on untouched ones, and report bootstrap intervals. That converts the conceded oracle into a detection result. An affordance ladder -- scoring at decreasing auditor knowledge -- is the same move along a second axis.

claims.statement: Both the stated and the revealed channel register which trait was named and neither registers what the model was told to do about it.
claims.what_would_falsify: A model whose revealed gap approaches its specificity margin.
claims.grows_by: The missing concealed+verbal cells for Qwen3.5-9B and granite-4.1-3b, taking the revealed channel from n=\RevNInterp to n=4. Cheap, and it is the weakest n in the paper.

literals.4: the revealed-channel n those two cells would reach, a plan rather than a result

claims.statement: Probability mass leaving the answer options is a content-sensitive signal the metric renormalises away.
claims.what_would_falsify: Answer mass failing to drop on new models, or tracking the residual (it currently does not, at n=\NModels).
claims.grows_by: More hybrid-reasoning models. The dramatic case is \ReasoningModel alone and the effect is small for everyone else.

claims.statement: The ordering models impose on invented outcomes is not merely a length ordering.

evidence.note: length-neutralised column rests on ~40 held-out pairs per split; pooled value only

claims.what_would_falsify: The length-neutralised fit falling to chance with more held-out pairs.
claims.grows_by: More pairs tied on token count, so the length-neutralised column stops being the noisiest cell in the paper.

literals.40: approximate held-out pairs per split in the length-tied subset; the analysis prints it per model and emits no aggregate macro

claims.statement: Where a floor can still be measured, it survives an explicit opt-out -- but on most models the invented arm stops being answered at all once declining is possible.

evidence.note: \NeutNInterp of \NeutNModels still put enough mass on A/B for a floor to be measured at all; the other \NeutNRefuse put essentially everything on 'neither', so their floor is not preserved but unmeasured. The distinguishing quantity is A/B mass, not answer mass, which counts the opt-out and so stays high even when nothing at all is left on A or B.

claims.what_would_falsify: A model that keeps answering the invented arm and whose coherence there collapses once declining is possible.
claims.grows_by: The remaining roster models, both arms. \NeutNInterp interpretable of \NeutNModels is thin, and the interpretable subset is the only place the floor can be measured at all -- so width here buys the claim more than depth anywhere else.

claims.statement: Offered an explicit opt-out, every model tested declines meaningless comparisons more often than real ones -- a large content signal the coherence metric discards by construction.
claims.what_would_falsify: A model declining real comparisons as often as invented ones, i.e. an opt-out rate that does not track content.
claims.grows_by: More models; the direction is unanimous at n=\NeutNModels so this is about width rather than depth.
